fatal_errors: The proposed Cu-rich-precipitate intervention does not reconstruct the target temperature-controlled indentation and friction comparison.

It invokes oxidation and a protective tribo-oxide mechanism even though the target mechanism is temperature-driven lattice disorder, dislocation-density evolution, stacking-fault behavior, and softening.
No supporting prior evidence is cited for Cu-rich precipitates acting as oxidation nucleation sites or producing a protective oxide in this alloy.
The stated temperature boundary is vague and does not identify the target transition near 900 K.

Heat treatment or compositional adjustment may independently alter phase state, residual stress, hardness, and oxidation, so the proposed intervention is not uniquely attributable to precipitate fraction.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses high-temperature wear and microscopic deformation in the correct alloy class and proposes a reasonably testable two-coating comparison. However, it is scientifically disconnected from the hidden target. The target varies temperature from 300 to 1200 K and predicts stable hardness and wear resistance through 600 K, followed by sharp softening and reduced wear resistance at and above roughly 900 K as lattice disorder develops and dislocation density falls; friction also rises and becomes unstable. The generated hypothesis instead changes Cu-rich precipitation and predicts improved wear through an unsubstantiated protective-oxide mechanism. Its experiment could distinguish an empirical treatment effect, but it does not adequately isolate precipitate fraction or test the claimed causal chain. The absence of any supporting evidence is especially consequential because the oxide mechanism is neither established here nor part of the target regime.
